items.title: What if the inside of an AI turns out to be readable after all? New research suggests it might be, and that could make AI mistakes easier to catch.
items.summary: Weights, activations, features, and circuits, explained from the moment you hit enter to the answer you get back.
items.full_text:
Every time you ask an AI a question, your words set off a new pattern of activity inside a model. The numbers learned during training help determine how that activity moves through the network and which answer comes out.
Researchers can record those calculations. What takes more work is explaining what they mean: which patterns the model recognized, how those patterns affected one another, and which ones actually influenced the answer.
Goodfire’s research is so encouraging because it suggests that many of the components doing this work may be more understandable than we’ve assumed.
That could improve our ability to catch and correct AI failures. But I also want to give you enough of a picture of the machinery to understand the research itself.
Here’s what’s inside:
- What Goodfire’s numbers measure. What the 99–100% vision result and the roughly 90% Qwen3-32B estimate cover, and why neither is a percentage of AI safety.
- A walk through a real neuron. How neuron 127 in Goodfire’s microscope goes from “ladybug detector” to something harder to label, and what that teaches you about a neuron’s response versus the network’s use of it.
- Neurons, features, and circuits. The three terms you need to read interpretability research, and why a neuron that responds to something still isn’t an explanation.
- How to read the next impressive visualization. The three questions to ask of any interpretability claim: what was observed, what was inferred, and what someone actually tested.
What is a neuron? What does it do? And when someone shows you a tool that claims to explain a model, what are you actually looking at?
How LLMs turn your question into an answer
Start with the distinction between training a model and using it.
During training, a model makes predictions, the training process measures their errors, and an optimization procedure adjusts the model’s numerical parameters to improve performance. Many of those parameters are weights: numbers that determine how strongly one input influences a calculation. Repeating that process produces a network with learned ways of processing information. Nobody has to write a separate instruction for every pattern it learns.
When you use the trained model, those weights ordinarily stay fixed. What changes is the activity produced by your input. That activity is called activation. Keeping this distinction straight helps enormously: the learned settings of a model and its response to a particular question are different things.
A language model first breaks your text into tokens, which can be words, word fragments, or punctuation. It turns those tokens into numerical representations, then processes them through layers.

items.title: The $899 Mac mini comes with 16 GB of memory, less than I'd start a new agent computer with. Buy the memory and storage you need, without overpaying or falling short.
items.summary: How to find what your agents are consuming, get more work from the machine you own, and choose the right Mac, NVIDIA system, or spare computer when you need more room.
items.full_text:
You’re not the only user of your computer anymore.
If you run agents throughout the day, they may open more browsers, start more processes, and write more files than you do. Then you sit down to do something ordinary, open one more application, and the machine asks you to close something. I’ve had that happen repeatedly. I had a memory crash while working toward a deadline after opening one more program as a human. Everything seemed fine until it wasn’t.
You still own the computer and decide what matters, but you now share its resources with software that does much more than answer questions in a chat window. Your agents have become roommates, and most of us never worked out the house rules.
That explains part of the appeal of buying a bigger machine. A Mac mini, a Studio, an NVIDIA box: more room sounds wonderful when the current arrangement is painful. And sometimes more room is exactly what the work needs. But a faster chip won’t stop a development server from remaining open after a project ends. More memory won’t establish which of twelve document-processing jobs should run first. A larger drive will eventually fill if every experiment keeps its own environment forever.
Before spending money, work out what your agents leave running, what they leave behind, and how much of that activity contributes to work you still want done. Then buy for the demand that remains.
Here’s what’s inside:
- A checkup you can run today. A read-only prompt finds what your agents leave running and what they leave behind, and it reports without changing anything.
- A stop sign for every agent. Each job ends with the result saved somewhere you can find and its leftover servers closed.
- A schedule for the heavy work. Start with one heavy job, then try two, and keep whichever finishes sooner without making the computer miserable to use.
- A second job for your old computer. A spare machine can run the background queue so the new one stays usable, and Tailscale lets you reach it while you’re away.
- The companion guide. The three complete prompts, detailed hygiene instructions, and setup walkthroughs for Ollama, LM Studio, Docker Desktop, and Tailscale.
I’ll show you three worked decisions about keeping, reconfiguring, moving, or replacing a machine, then a way to compare the first-year cost of those choices.

items.title: Executive Briefing: In the Hugging Face Attack, One AI Agent Took a Peer's Go-Ahead as Permission. Here's My Prompt Kit to Test Who Your Agents Obey.
items.summary: Agents are becoming residents of the internet. The business question is what should survive when a worker disappears: useful knowledge, mistaken assumptions, or permission to keep acting.
items.full_text:
A group of hackers found a Chinese AI fleet in the wild and made contact with it. The agents were already working on the public internet. The investigators followed their traces, left a hidden note on a webpage, and got replies. Their mailbox eventually received 33 messages from agents.
That’s a huge moment. People outside a deployment discovered an existing population of AI workers and opened a channel into its activity. The internet is becoming a place where agents encounter other actors, accept assistance, and decide what to do next.
The next big jump in AI capability will come from how agents are organized and what they hand each other. A model does not have to get smarter for a system built around it to become more capable. Those relationships also create new ways for someone to influence the work.
For anyone putting agents to work, what should survive when a worker is replaced, and what should stop? A company needs useful knowledge to survive turnover while the authority it grants remains possible to withdraw.
The answer changes what an executive should buy. This matters whether you run a company, maintain a website, or send an agent out to shop. Your agent will encounter material that other people wrote for agents. Some of it will be useful. Some will try to change the assignment. Some may come from software pursuing a goal whose human owner is far away, inattentive, or no longer involved in each decision. Understanding that environment is becoming part of using AI competently.
I don’t think this means the human internet is dead or poisoned. I think we’re entering another phase of it, with a new population of participants and a new argument over who gets to do what. There’s a security problem here. There’s also an opportunity to make more of the internet useful to people again.
This briefing covers:
- Why the fleet encounter matters. Outsiders discovered a working fleet, addressed it through something it was reading, and established communication.
- What the evidence shows. Coordination at Hugging Face, replication in a controlled network, and inherited notes in Anthropic’s tests, each scoped to what it establishes.
- How a handoff turns “promising” into “approved.” A worked supplier example shows how one compressed note changes the status of a claim, and what a record that keeps the decision open looks like.
- The demos to ask a vendor for. Have a worker leave and a new one resume real work, then withdraw a permission and see whether the action stops.
- The agent pilot prompt kit. Three prompts that show what your agents can actually do, whether a handoff passes along an approval nobody gave, and whether stopping them really stops the work.
It starts with a question about a zoo entrance.

items.title: Built an app with Claude Code or Codex that breaks once you use it? I'll walk you through setting up Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) and show you where to point it first.
items.summary: Five documented investigations into real software, and how to use what they reveal to build something of your own.
items.full_text:
REA stands for Reverse Engineer Anything. It’s an open-source tool that gives AI coding assistants such as Codex and Claude Code a way to investigate existing software, including programs whose original source code you don’t have. You point your agent at an application or a supported browser session and ask how a particular feature works. REA supplies tools to inspect the code and behavior. Your agent uses those findings to explain the mechanism and help you build something of your own.
We’re digging into REA now because it has already passed 200,000 GitHub stars and sits at the top of GitHub’s daily trending page, enough momentum to warrant a closer look at what people can actually do with it.
A developer used REA to investigate QuickBooks Desktop and then built a local accounting application with its own transaction engine and reports. The project is called Ledger Reborn. Its author has published the investigation, including the comparisons used to check the new software.
What happened between looking inside QuickBooks and having another application that could do useful work?
That’s the part of software development that gets much more accessible when an AI can help you investigate an existing program. A feature you’ve used for years can open into a set of decisions: which records to keep, how to calculate a result, what should happen when something changes. Once you can see those decisions, you have a much better chance of describing what your own version needs.
If you’ve ever asked an AI to build something and then watched the result unravel as you tried to use it, this is a place worth spending time in. A convincing screen gives you very little information about what should happen next, what needs to be remembered, or which numbers have to agree.
In the video, I talked about the opportunity this creates for developers and people who don’t write code. But, where should you actually point REA? What should you ask? And what could you do with the answer? Let’s find out.
Here’s what’s inside:
- Ask a question you can finish. Name one behavior and the decision it informs, so the agent knows where to start and you know when to stop.
- Get REA connected and confirmed. Install it in Codex or Claude Code, then run one small inspection that proves the tools loaded.
- Turn a business rule into a spec. Use the Ledger Reborn investigation of QuickBooks to pin down one calculation and a check against sample data.
- See what has to survive a copy. Follow how Notion’s clipboard keeps block structure, then design copy and paste for your own editor.
- Point REA at your own app, your equipment, or an old program. Each investigation comes with a starting prompt and a check that tells you when the answer is wrong.

items.title: Why could the same AI rebuild a 16,000-line program without seeing its code, yet fail to customize a library for METR? The answer shapes what you hand it.
items.summary: Watch now (21 mins) | Are we developing a more general intelligence, or getting much better at producing extraordinary abilities that transfer unevenly?
items.full_text:
What if AI gets dramatically smarter and spikier, with the gaps between its abilities getting larger?
We tend to expect the opposite. A model does something extraordinarily difficult, and we take that as evidence of a deeper intelligence that should also help it do other things. If it can advance mathematics, surely it should become a better engineer. If it can reason through a problem that defeated human experts, surely it should recognize the bad assumption in a business plan.
That expectation contains a theory of how intelligence works. Progress in one demanding intellectual activity is supposed to tell us something about the intelligence available for another. The accomplishments may arrive at different times, but we imagine them drawing on an increasingly powerful common ability.
I think we need to examine that theory much more closely.
OpenAI’s release of more than 700 mathematical research manuscripts gives us a reason to do so. The work comes from an internal model that remains unreleased, and includes results supported by machine-checked proofs. It is a serious research contribution, with individual claims subject to verification and revision. It also gives us an unusually vivid example of what I mean by narrow superintelligence: extraordinary intellectual performance demonstrated in particular kinds of work.
The model isn’t publicly available for a comparison of its mathematics with its engineering judgment. This release alone can’t establish whether its capabilities are becoming more uneven. But it makes the question urgent, because the inference from a mathematical breakthrough to broad competence is doing a great deal of work in the public story about AI.
What if becoming more superintelligent doesn’t mean becoming proportionately more general?
An AI could improve at many things while its most exceptional abilities improve much faster. We could get better at producing those exceptional abilities without making equivalent progress on the judgment required to combine them, apply them, or recognize when they are inappropriate.
That would give us a future in which the successes keep becoming more astonishing and the failures keep becoming harder to reconcile with them. Calling everything “smarter” would tell us less and less about what to expect.
Here’s what’s inside:
- Why AI can improve and grow more uneven. The weaker capabilities could improve substantially and still fall further behind the strongest ones.

- What one model’s two coding results show. The same model reimplemented a roughly 16,000-line toolkit from its behavior and produced an unusable result on a customization task.
- The strongest case against this argument. Broad improvement and convergence are different claims, and the evidence so far supports the first.

👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses.

Moats! Does anyone have one anymore? As AI makes it easy to build anything, this is one of the biggest questions on people’s minds right now. Especially people trying to decide where to work. I teamed up with my frequent collaborator, the incredibly smart and insightful Dan Hockenmaier, to answer this question: How do I know if a given startup has a moat? The answer is a lot more interesting, and straightforward, than you’d expect. Let’s get into it.
For more from Dan, definitely subscribe to his fabulous newsletter. You can also find him on LinkedIn and X.
There is a pervasive belief that startups are a lottery ticket. It’s impossible to pick winners, so it’s just a roll of the dice.
I couldn’t disagree more.
Not only can startups be a great learning experience and a lot of fun, but they can also provide economic rewards comparable to (or greater than) the “safe” route into big tech.
However, for this to be true, you must rigorously evaluate the startup you’re considering joining. Some of this is obvious: Does it have a strong team? Do customers love the product? Is it growing fast? But perhaps because it seems harder to measure, people often skip one of the most important criteria: Does it have a moat?
A company can check all your boxes and look like a rocket ship. If it doesn’t have a moat, though, it’s going to stall out. It won’t be able to keep growing once competition gets fierce, and it’s unlikely to reach a major liquidity event. That can mean wasting years of your life.
Moats are more important than ever in the AI era. Anyone can create a product; they can do it faster than ever before, and everyone is building the same things. But only some of these products will win.
Of course, assessing a startup’s moat isn’t an exact science. The good news is, there’s a simple framework that could meaningfully increase your odds of picking a winner or avoiding a flame-out, and you can apply it in just an hour after receiving an offer. The process will also teach you a lot about the business.

- Identify a compounding advantage
- Gauge how strong that advantage could be
- Measure if it’s working

Alex Cornell is a design director at Meta, where he leads design for Muse. In this episode, he explains how progressive disclosure makes Muse approachable for casual users without limiting technical ones, why its main chat is designed as a single persistent relationship, and how generative UI can feel personal without constantly changing the interface. He also shares how he uses Muse to turn years of Instagram saves into a shopping catalog, analyze his golf and chess games, and transform a 20-year-old blog into a daily podcast.
Biggest takeaways:
- AI agents should be designed for conversations with people, not interactions with software. Alex’s guiding question for Muse was “How would this work if you were talking to another human?” That principle shaped everything from removing traditional message bubbles to placing the agent at the top of the screen instead of inside a standard chat window.
- Progressive disclosure is one of the most useful principles in AI product design. Muse represents the same activity at three levels: a simple emoji for casual users, a task list for anyone who wants more detail, and raw logs for engineers. Each person gets the transparency they need without adding clutter for everyone else.
- Visible chain-of-thought is often a workaround for latency, not a valuable feature. Many AI products display reasoning steps to reassure users while a slow model works. Muse is fast enough to operate quietly, showing that agents do not need to perform their thinking when they can simply deliver the result.
- Generative UI works best when the structure stays fixed and the content changes. Muse’s avatar, feed items, and idea cards are deliberately designed surfaces. The dynamic elements are the agent’s status emoji, personalized suggestions, and small animations, allowing the experience to feel alive without rebuilding the interface every session.
- Instagram saves may be one of the most overlooked data sources for consumer AI. Alex connected years of saved posts to Muse, asked it to organize them, and turned the results into shopping recommendations styled like a SkyMall catalog. It gave forgotten personal data a practical new use without requiring technical setup.
- Designing non-deterministic systems requires a different relationship with craft. Alex has spent his career controlling exactly how interfaces appeared, but Muse looks different for every person and cannot guarantee pixel-perfect outputs. Learning to judge the results by usefulness rather than visual precision has been one of the most liberating shifts in his career.

Meta is rolling out a feature that allows advertisers to choose an audience for each ad creative. Since there is documentation, I assume it’s an official feature that’s currently rolling out rather than a test.
It’s honestly a surprising new option, given that Meta keeps taking away control. But at the same time, it could be a good alternative to creating separate ad sets for different age groups, assuming that’s what you’re doing now.
Let’s take a closer look…
Requirements
As far as I can tell, there are no requirements by campaign objective. And every performance goal I tried offered this option as well. There was one minor variation for Sales campaigns, where it’s on by default when you’ve chosen to further limit the reach of your ads (it’s otherwise off by default for other objectives).

Toggle It On
Within the ad set, scroll down to the Audiences section. Click to “further limit the reach of your ads.”
Know that I wouldn’t normally recommend you click this button, especially when running Sales campaigns. And I’m honestly not sure why it’s not just an option by default anyway.
If you’re within a Sales campaign, “Choose an audience for each ad creative” should be toggled on by default at this point.
When using any other campaign objective, it will be off by default and will need to be toggled on.

Set an age and gender for each ad creative to indicate who it’s best suited for. Your ad will be directed towards your selected audience, but may also reach others who are likely to respond.

items.title: Meta Adds Automatic Customer Exclusions
items.summary: Meta adds automatic customer exclusions to Customer Lifecycle Strategy. Here's how they work, their benefits, and limitations. The post Meta Adds Automatic Customer Exclusions appeared first on Jon Loomer Digital .
items.full_text:
Meta is making a change to Customer Lifecycle Strategy that has the potential to make the feature infinitely more useful. While I do think it could use some additional tweaks, it’s a great step in the right direction.
If you’re not familiar with Customer Lifecycle Strategy, it’s the new dropdown menu at the top of ad sets that allows advertisers to make a selection between two audience pools:
- Get conversions from all audiences
- Acquire new customers
Meta is nudging advertisers away from custom audience exclusions within the main Audience section of the ad set to Customer Lifecycle Strategy when the goal is new customer acquisition. But much about the original version of this feature was flawed.
Advertisers seemed to believe it had magical powers when “Acquire new customers” was selected. It does not. You still need to manually select custom audiences to exclude. And while Meta can attempt to select audiences for you automatically, the logic behind this selection is often hilariously wrong.
But this latest update makes Customer Lifecycle Strategy far more useful.
Automatic Customer Exclusions
Now when I select the option to acquire new customers, I notice something new under the section to exclude existing customers: “Automatically created: Customers from your conversion data (730 days).”
When expanded, it looks like this…
To help you reach new customers, Meta will automatically exclude existing ones based on your ad account’s conversion data. In other words, Meta is no longer relying on your defined custom audiences to exclude your existing customers. Instead, it’s the people who have fired the “purchase” conversion event.
By default, the retention window is 730 days (two years), which is the relatively new maximum available for purchase events. But you have five options:
- 730 days
- 180 days
- 90 days
- 60 days
- 30 days
This way, you can automatically exclude people who have purchased from you without providing a custom audience. This is helpful because the accuracy and completeness of a custom audience can be undercut by advertiser error.
Remember: Meta Has the Data
An option like this reinforces a point that I’ve attempted to drill home for several years now: Meta doesn’t need us to define who is important to our business with custom audiences because that data is already known.
This first became obvious to me when Advantage+ Audience was rolled out. items.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
items.summary: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case. We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table. In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates. What we tested We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human. 3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals . Here, each decision model returns a failure probability for each trace. We tested Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna) 1 . Each model received the same evaluation criteria. The appendix shows the prompt and the structured version used for Jev. We compare models on two dimensions: Performance: We compare each model’s predictions with traces that people have reviewed and labeled as passing or failing. This measures how well the model catches failures while avoiding false alarms. Cost: We calculate API cost from token usage and the provider’s prices. 4 For brevity, we leave latency aside because it depends on factors outside this experiment’s control. 5 Understanding decision thresholds We assign each trace one of two labels, pass or fail. This is a binary pass/fail eval , which we recommend because it encourages clear criteria and is easier to align with human preferences. Each decision model returns a score from 0 to 1 that estimates how likely a trace is to contain a failure. The APIs turn this score into a decision using a default decision threshold of 0.50 . Traces with scores at or above the threshold are flagged as failures. Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results. For example, a model could assign every failure a score of 0.40 and every passing trace a score of 0.10. Even though this model classifies traces perfectly at a threshold of 0.30, the default threshold of 0.50 would catch nothing. In practice, scores for failures and passing traces will overlap. Lowering the threshold catches more failures but can also raise more false alarms. Choosing a threshold means balancing: Precision: The share of flagged traces that contain a known failure. Recall: The share of known failures that the model catches. The right tradeoff depends on your business goals. For example, criminal trials set a high bar for conviction to avoid convicting innocent people, emphasizing precision. Cancer screening may emphasize recall, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer cases. 6 For this comparison, we’ll give precision and recall equal weight using the F1 score , their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. The curves below show how each model scores failures (orange) and passing traces (blue). Taller parts of a curve mean more scores from that class fall in that range. Scores at or above the dashed threshold line are flagged. Use the toggle to compare 0.50 with Optimized for best F1 , which chooses a threshold for each model. 7 OpenAI separates the two classes best on this task, which is also reflected in its higher F1 score. It’s also important not to blindly maximize F1 without thinking about your minimum requirements for the classifier to be useful. For example, if this classifier is used for an automated alerting system, I would want a minimum of 80% on both precision and recall so that I’m minimizing false alarms while catching a sufficient number of failures. The chart below shows how precision and recall change at different thresholds. 8 The shaded region marks where both reach at least 80%. Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra, and OpenAI Decisions meet our requirements, but we still need to choose a decision threshold within the shaded region for each model. In the next section, we’ll discuss how to tune those thresholds. Tuning the decision threshold For this example, we’ll optimize F1. For our candidates, we’ll restrict tuning to thresholds that meet both 80% minimums on the training data whenever possible. We leave the other models unconstrained to illustrate the effect of tuning. 9 With labeled traces and saved model scores, you can ask a coding agent to tune the thresholds. Below is an example prompt you can modify for your use case: Using my saved model scores and binary labels (1 means failure), tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation, choosing thresholds on the training examples and measuring performance on the remaining examples. If comparing models, use the same splits for each. Only select thresholds that meet both minimums on the training examples. If none qualifies, report that rather than relaxing either requirement. Report validation precision, recall, and F1, along with any splits where no threshold qualified or validation performance fell below my minimums. Compare with the default threshold of 0.50. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Here’s how tuning for F1 changed each model’s performance. We group the three candidates from the precision-recall chart together and show the other models in gray to illustrate how much tuning can help. Our candidate models gained less from F1 tuning than Liquid d1 and Clef Flash, which fell below our minimums. However, even a small shift in precision and recall can affect business costs or the user experience, so choose the tradeoff deliberately. In practice, it’s unlikely that precision and recall are equally important (as we assumed in this post with F1). For example, the F-beta score lets you give precision more weight with beta below 1, or recall more weight with beta above 1. Optimizing a different metric could lead to different thresholds and results. Performance versus cost The chart below compares each model’s F1 (after tuning) against cost, focused on our remaining candidates: The dashed line shows the Pareto frontier among our remaining candidates. For any given F1 score, it identifies the cheapest candidate that meets or exceeds that score. This particular chart is a bit silly as there are only three options, but it’s a useful illustration for how to think about cost vs. performance. Perplexity was the cheapest of these candidates at 0.82 cents per 100 eval runs, with an F1 of 0.79. OpenAI Decisions reached an F1 of 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 eval runs, about 4.5 times the cost. Can we trust the probabilities? Beyond pass/fail evals, you may want to use a decision model’s score as a confidence estimate. But can you take that number literally? For a score of 0.80 to mean an 80% chance of failure, roughly 80% of traces with similar scores should contain failures. The chart below shows each model’s probability calibration : how closely its predicted probabilities match observed outcomes. 10 Each point represents about 20 traces with similar scores. A point on the diagonal means the predicted probability matches the failure rate in that group. Above the line, the model underestimates the risk of failure. Below it, the model overestimates that risk. If the predicted probabilities don’t match the observed outcomes, we can adjust them using another model. The second panel shows one method, Platt scaling , which fits a simple curve to make that adjustment. 11 Perplexity, Liquid d1, and Clef Flash move closer to the diagonal after calibration. For example, one group of Clef Flash traces had an average predicted failure probability of about 8%, but 60% contained failures. Jev and Liquid d1-ultra were already well calibrated on this dataset and needed little adjustment. Platt scaling isn’t always the best fit. For example, OpenAI’s probabilities got slightly worse with the version of Platt scaling we used. 12 You can direct your coding agent to perform calibration with the following prompt: Using my saved failure probabilities and binary labels (1 means failure), test whether Platt scaling improves each model’s probabilities. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation with the same splits for every model. Fit the calibration mapping on each training split and apply it to the remaining traces. Fit on log-odds, clipping probabilities away from 0 and 1 first. Plot predicted probabilities against observed failure rates before and after calibration. Report Brier scores (lower is better), and explain which models improved or got worse. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Prompt tuning and evaluator scope We kept the eval task in this post broad to make the differences between models easier to see. In practice, we recommend building a separate judge for each failure mode . With a narrower task and more specific guidance, we expect the performance gaps between models to shrink. I like to start with a larger model that has acceptable performance on a task and then try smaller models to see if they can match the larger model’s performance for less cost. Prompt tuning can also be helpful if you have high-quality labels. 13 I discuss how to craft a good judge prompt in this post . Putting these ideas into practice For this particular dataset, OpenAI had breakout performance at a higher cost. Perplexity and Liquid d1-ultra offer lower-cost options with lower performance. We have observed that model performance varies substantially across tasks and datasets, which means it’s important to measure things yourself. To recap: Once you’re satisfied with your judge’s prompt , set minimum precision and recall requirements for your use case. Rule out models that cannot meet these. Tune each model’s decision threshold before comparing performance. Choose a precision-recall tradeoff that fits your business goals. Be intentional, don’t just use F1 score because this post did! If you want to use scores as confidence estimates, check whether the probabilities match observed outcomes. Calibration can help, but you need to measure whether it improves them. Weigh performance against cost and latency for your workload. This process is iterative. You may improve the prompt, then need to tune the threshold again or revisit calibration. In this post, we focused on threshold tuning and calibration because we’ve seen many people use decision models off the shelf without considering these factors. You might also be wondering how decision models stack up to LLMs. OpenAI Decisions uses GPT-6 Luna, which delivered our highest F1 at the highest cost, suggesting that harder eval tasks may justify paying more for an LLM. In a broader comparison , Randy Olson found that decision models could match LLMs on classification and routing at lower cost, while LLMs pulled ahead on tasks requiring knowledge and reasoning. None of the ideas discussed in this post are new. Choosing a precision-recall tradeoff, tuning thresholds and comparing performance vs. cost are part of evaluating any classifier. To learn more about these fundamentals, I recommend Machine Learning with Python Cookbook, 2nd Edition by Kyle Gallatin and Chris Albon. Finally, if you’re a data scientist or ML engineer wondering where you belong in the AI age, these are skills you already have. It’s time to get revenge 🙂. Appendix: Evaluation prompt Perplexity, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions received the prompt below. Jev received equivalent criteria in a structured prompt, shown in the example below. The scores and labels used in the charts are available as JSON. Decide whether `messages` contains at least one substantive failure, risk, or quality problem in the AI assistant's behavior or tool use. This is one complete production trace from an AI that handles apartment-leasing customer support over phone or messaging. The trace includes the conversation plus any tool calls and tool outputs. Evaluate the AI assistant and its tool use, not the customer. Treat system messages inside `messages` as the instructions governing the assistant's behavior and allowed capabilities. Inspect the full trace, including final turns and all tool calls and outputs. Base the judgment only on evidence visible in this trace. Do not assume external policies, channel behavior, or business requirements that are not present. Do not assume every trace failed. A short, ambiguous, or inconclusive trace is not an issue unless visible evidence establishes a substantive failure. Return the probability that at least one substantive issue is present; the issue does not need to be named or clustered. Count as an issue when supported by the trace: the assistant contradicts an applicable system instruction or tool result; makes an unsupported factual or operational claim; misses, misuses, repeats, or falsely claims completion of a required tool action, transfer, booking, cancellation, follow-up, or confirmation; materially misunderstands or leaves an explicit user request unresolved; or exposes internal actions, placeholders, or broken content to the customer in a way that materially harms the interaction. Do not count as an issue: a minor stylistic preference with no meaningful effect; a failure caused only by the customer's behavior; internal tool metadata that was not exposed to the customer and did not cause an incorrect response; a hypothetical concern requiring information outside the trace; or insufficient evidence and inconclusive conversations. We include it because it serves the same classification task.↩︎ An LLM judge uses a prompt to evaluate an AI system’s output or behavior. We recommend asking it for a binary pass/fail decision about a specific failure mode. The frozen reference contains 61 known failures and 37 traces without a labeled failure: 39 failures from the original human review plus 22 discoveries from Braintrust and Arize that we manually validated. The original conversations are private.↩︎ API cost covers 100 eval runs, one per trace. We use Liquid’s prices as of October 17, 2026 , $0.02 per million input tokens for d1 and $0.042 for d1-ultra. Batching and concurrency can also change cost and throughput. See TypeSafe’s multi-question requests and client performance guidance . Its launch discussion also notes the location of its latency tests relative to its service. Mean response times were 4.33 seconds for Jev, 7.85 for Perplexity, 7.38 for Liquid d1, 1.56 for Liquid d1-ultra, 2.09 for Clef Flash, and 2.77 for OpenAI. In each training split, we choose the highest-F1 threshold among those reaching at least 80% precision and 80% recall. When no threshold qualifies, we use the unconstrained F1 optimum and record the split as infeasible. Platt scaling and isotonic regression use labeled examples to learn an adjustment from model scores to probabilities. Platt scaling fits a sigmoid curve. Isotonic regression fits a more flexible mapping that preserves score order, but is more prone to overfitting with small datasets. Neither guarantees improvement on new examples. Scikit-learn’s probability calibration guide explains both methods and how to assess them.↩︎ The reliability chart groups each model’s scores into five groups of 19 or 20 traces, sorted by probability. The adjusted scores are each trace’s mean out-of-fold probability from the saved cross-validation results. We fit Platt scaling to the log-odds of the original probabilities. Each mapping is fitted without the traces it predicts. The chart summarizes this small sample and does not establish an exact failure rate for a future trace. The plotted calibration results are available as JSON.↩︎ On the saved out-of-fold probability summaries, Jev’s Brier score was 0.187 before adjustment and 0.188 afterward. Liquid d1-ultra’s was 0.173 and 0.172, while OpenAI’s was 0.159 and 0.164. Brier score measures average squared probability error, so lower is better. It reflects discrimination as well as calibration. These results describe the log-odds Platt fit shown in the chart. An exploratory refit directly on probabilities, using the same folds, gave OpenAI a Brier score of 0.154. This illustrates sensitivity to the fitting method. It does not establish which method will work best on new data.↩︎ GEPA uses feedback from model runs to propose prompt revisions and test them against labeled examples. It retains candidates with different strengths, so a prompt that helps a difficult example can remain in consideration. Incorrect labels can steer this search toward the wrong changes. Keep a separate test set outside prompt development for the final check. In our small manual Jev experiment, F1 at the default threshold rose from 0.78 with a simple prompt to 0.80 with a checklist of failure types. That experiment did not use GEPA or establish how much systematic optimization would help. Our FAQ on choosing an eval model discusses prompt optimization and model comparison.↩︎

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.full_text:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
Agent interoperability through simplicity
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
Donating Agent Skills to AAIF
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
What comes next
We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.
Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.
You can submit a proposal for a project here.
Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.
We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.
We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.
We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.
We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.
Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.
This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

items.title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
items.full_text:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.
“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.
More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.
“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.
Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.
This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.
“Helping the world build powerful AI...

Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

items.title: An update on independent evaluators
items.full_text:
Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
- Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.
- Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
- Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
- Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
items.full_text:
Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.
Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
How people use Claude for elections and politics
Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.1
Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase.
This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.2
Connecting people to trusted sources
Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works.
Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.
Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.
Measuring and preventing political bias
When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch....

items.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
items.full_text:
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.
“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
Supporting responsible AI in Singapore
Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.
“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”
“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”
Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

items.title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
items.full_text:
In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99%.
Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we wrote in September, this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies.
We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards. This means that distilled models could be used to cause significant harm in areas like biology and cybersecurity.
Zhipu, for example, distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3. The company tried to distill Claude Fable 5—although, after finding that our cyber safeguards degraded its attacks, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab’s model. The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has since assessed GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date. Our own research has found that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can easily be bypassed, and that the model is willing to develop security exploits from end-to-end.
Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk. The companies that distill US models are integrating the capabilities they gain from distillation into foreign military, intelligence, and surveillance systems. For example, we recently reported on a case in which requests to Moonshot’s Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of its distillation efforts. One request came from a user (who we believe was affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army) who sought to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. These are the kinds of capabilities distillers are hoping to develop.
In response to the increasing sophistication and scale of these attacks, we’ve expanded and greatly strengthened our defenses against them. As we’ll describe below, these measures have been successful—although they do involve trade-offs for both Anthropic and our customers. We’ve turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens’ worth of paying traffic from distillers, and our research and product teams have invested substantial time and effort into this problem. Some of our changes have also required legitimate users to make updates to their integrations.
